headline: 10-year-old builds InfinityOS 13.0 with offline AI after sacrificing 10 motherboards
summary: A 10-year-old developer from India has created InfinityOS 13.0, a custom Linux-based operating system, featuring an integrated offline AI called InfinityX AI, built using llama.cpp.
details: A 10-year-old from Udaipur, India, has developed InfinityOS 13.0, a full operating system ecosystem. This impressive project includes an offline AI, InfinityX AI, built using llama.cpp, that runs entirely without an internet connection.

The young developer learned BIOS recovery by bricking 10 motherboards, leading to the creation of SkyBIOS. This open firmware is based on coreboot, with a deep understanding of the romstage -> ramstage bootflow.
InfinityOS is powered by the Infinity Kernel, a custom Linux kernel tailored for the operating system. It provides the foundational layer for the entire system.
The ecosystem also features the Infinity Installer, a custom OS installer designed by the developer. This tool facilitates the installation of InfinityOS onto user machines.
For customization, the Infinity ISO Studio allows users to build their own custom ISOs. This tool is powered by xorriso, offering flexibility in system deployment.
The standout feature, InfinityX AI, is an offline AI solution integrated directly into InfinityOS. It leverages llama.cpp to provide AI capabilities without relying on external network access.

headline_marked: IBM CEO: [[Open weight models are now 90% as effective for 10% the cost]] on-prem
headline: IBM CEO: Open weight models are now 90% as effective for 10% the cost on-prem
summary: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna stated that open weight models now offer 90% of the performance of frontier models at just 10% of the cost, making them highly attractive for on-premise enterprise use.
details: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna highlighted open weight models' cost-effectiveness on the Q3 earnings call. He noted they deliver 90% of the performance of frontier models at 10-25% of the token cost, making them "irresistibly good and cheap" for on-premise enterprise use. This significant cost advantage is driving enterprise interest.

Krishna explained that the performance gap between closed frontier models and open alternatives has significantly narrowed. While once a 70 vs. 20-30 score, by late 2025 it was 70 vs. 50, making the cost-benefit ratio of open models highly compelling.

For most enterprise tasks like summarizing emails, examining contracts, or answering customer calls, the CEO believes the cheaper open models are equally effective. This leads businesses to question paying ten times more for a marginal performance increase.

IBM is observing a surge in demand for on-prem AI infrastructure, with many businesses aiming to build useful systems in just two or three racks. However, Krishna acknowledged that enterprises often lack the specialized kernel and network engineers needed for complex deployments.

To address these deployment challenges, IBM plans to develop software solutions. Krishna also anticipates that the growing demand for on-prem AI will boost sales of Big Blue's Spyre mainframe accelerator cards, leveraging their existing hardware strengths.
